attack_mechanism: `openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_din` controls that execution sequencing before the frontend selects the next PC update; the state and data choices on this path depend on `openMSP430.frontend_0.pc_sw_wr`. The hardware dependence follows `openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_din -> openMSP430.dbg_0.halt_cpu -> openMSP430.frontend_0.e_first_state -> openMSP430.frontend_0.pc_nxt -> openMSP430.frontend_0.pc`. Instruction fetch is released from `I_DEC` only when `exec_done` or `E_IDLE` is observed, and `e_state` also determines whether jump, source-write, or destination-write completion is pending. A fault on `openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_din` can falsely complete an instruction or hold the execution machine in an earlier phase when `pc_nxt` is evaluated. The PC is advanced too early, held too long, or updated with operands belonging to the wrong instruction phase.

`openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_din` affects `fetch`, instruction length, or the instruction-state decision used by this sequential increment; the state and data choices on this path depend on `openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_rst`, `openMSP430.dbg_0.mem_data_wr`, `openMSP430.dbg_0.mem_bw`, `openMSP430.execution_unit_0.dbg_halt_st`, and the remaining path guards. With no software PC write and no interrupt-vector state active, `pc_nxt` falls through to `pc_incr = pc + {14'h0, fetch, 1'b0}`. Injecting a transient or stuck fault into `openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_din` before `pc` is enabled can add the wrong increment or prevent the expected increment. The next instruction is skipped, repeated, or fetched from an unintended address.

`openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_din` participates in forming or qualifying that software-PC path; the state and data choices on this path depend on `openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_rst`, `openMSP430.dbg_0.mem_addr_wr`, `openMSP430.frontend_0.cpu_halt_st`, `openMSP430.execution_unit_0.register_file_0.pc_sw_wr`. During a CALL, jump, or instruction that writes R0, `pc_sw_wr` has priority in the `pc_nxt` multiplexer and selects `pc_sw`. A transient bit flip or forced value on `openMSP430.dbg_0.dbg_din` before the next `mclk` edge can substitute a false target or assert the software-write selection on the wrong instruction. The corrupted target is captured in `pc`, redirecting control flow, skipping intended instructions, or executing an unintended basic block.
